clinicalPearls: Acute respiratory tract infection caused by Bordetella pertussis; 'pertussis' means 'violent cough' and the inspiratory whoop at the end of a paroxysm gives the disease its common name (p.1276).

Classic course runs through three stages: catarrhal phase (1-2 weeks of coryza, lacrimation, mild cough, low-grade fever, malaise, indistinguishable from a common cold), then paroxysmal phase (frequent spasmodic bursts of 5-10 coughs within a single expiration), then convalescent phase (p.1278-1279).
Paroxysms may end in an audible whoop produced by rapid inspiration against a closed glottis; post-tussive vomiting is frequent and a mucous plug may be expelled (p.1279).

During a coughing spasm there may be neck-vein distension, bulging eyes, tongue protrusion, and cyanosis; paroxysms can be precipitated by noise, eating, or physical contact and are often worse at night (p.1279).
Between attacks the patient looks normal but shows increasing fatigue; fever is uncommon and, when present, suggests bacterial superinfection (p.1279).
The convalescent phase lasts 1-3 months with gradual resolution; for 6-12 months afterward, intercurrent viral infections may trigger a recrudescence of paroxysmal cough (p.1279).
The whoop is variable: uncommon in infants 6 months of age or younger and frequently absent in older children and adults (p.1276).
Lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count >108-109/L) is common in young children and unusual with other infections, but is not a feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279).
Highly communicable: attack rates of 80-100% among unimmunized household contacts; cyclical outbreaks occur every 3-5 years despite widespread immunization (p.1277).
Severe morbidity and high mortality are restricted almost entirely to infants; in the US (2000-2017) infants under 2 months accounted for 84% of pertussis deaths (p.1278).
harrison.pathophysiology: Infection begins with attachment of B. pertussis to ciliated epithelial cells of the nasopharynx, mediated by surface adhesins (pertactin, filamentous hemagglutinin) binding integrin-family proteins, probably with pertussis toxin. The organism multiplies locally and produces toxins causing mucosal damage (tracheal cytotoxin, dermonecrotic toxin); host defense is impaired by pertussis toxin and adenylate cyclase-hemolysin toxin. There is local cellular invasion with intracellular persistence, but systemic dissemination does NOT occur; systemic manifestations such as lymphocytosis result from the toxins. The cause of the hallmark paroxysmal cough is not known; a pivotal role for pertussis toxin has been proposed but not confirmed. Neurologic events (seizures, encephalopathy) are thought to result from hypoxia due to coughing paroxysms or apnea rather than from specific bacterial products. Deaths in young infants are frequently associated with very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension (p.1278).
additionalDifferentials: Bordetella parapertussis (causes a similar but typically milder illness; does not express pertussis toxin gene) (p.1276).
Bordetella holmesii (found in up to 20% of patients with a pertussis-like syndrome using improved PCR) (p.1276).
Influenza virus and other respiratory viruses (p.1280).
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus -- isolated from patients with clinical pertussis but probably represent co-infection, particularly in children under 1 year (p.1280).
infectionMimics: Adenovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viral infections (p.1280)
additionalInvestigations: Nasopharyngeal culture (Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium) -- gold standard owing to 100% specificity; cultures become positive by day 5 of incubation (p.1279).

PCR / multitarget real-time PCR -- has replaced culture in most laboratories due to greater sensitivity and faster (hours) results; differentiates B. pertussis, B. parapertussis, and B. holmesii (p.1279).
Nasopharyngeal aspiration is the best specimen; B. pertussis is highly sensitive to drying so specimens must be inoculated without delay or placed in transport medium (p.1279).
Complete blood count for lymphocytosis (informative in young children, not in adolescents/adults) (p.1279).

Serology -- enzyme immunoassays for IgA/IgG to pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae; increasingly used in adolescents, adults, and those symptomatic >4 weeks; single-specimen anti-pertussis-toxin serology is becoming standardized, especially for outbreaks and surveillance (p.1279).
redFlags: Apnea in infants (occurred in 27.1% of children under 2 years hospitalized with pertussis) (p.1279).
Seizures and encephalopathy, thought to result from hypoxia of paroxysms/apnea (p.1278-1279).
Very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension in young infants -- frequently associated with death (p.1278).
Pneumonia (occurs in up to 22% of infants with pertussis) (p.1278-1279).
Infants, especially those under 2-3 months, carry the highest risk of complications and death and should generally be hospitalized (p.1278, 1279).
harrison.prognosis: With universal childhood immunization, reported cases fell by >90% and mortality declined even more dramatically. Severe morbidity and high mortality remain almost entirely restricted to infants; WHO estimates ~40 million cases and ~400,000 deaths globally each year, mostly among infants under 3 months. Immunity after natural infection is NOT lifelong; immunity after whole-cell vaccination is short-lived (little protection after 10-12 years) and wanes even faster (within 2-4 years of the fifth or sixth dose) in those immunized with acellular vaccines (p.1277-1278).
pitfalls: In adolescents and adults the presentation is often atypical -- frequently no paroxysmal cough or whoop -- so pertussis is a commonly missed cause of prolonged cough; B. pertussis may be the agent in 12-30% of adults whose cough does not improve within 2 weeks (p.1278).
Antibiotic therapy aims to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage; it does NOT substantially alter the clinical course unless given early in the catarrhal phase (p.1279).
Cough suppressants are NOT effective and have no role in management; beta-adrenergic agonists and glucocorticoids have been advocated but are NOT proven effective (p.1280).
Lymphocytosis is helpful in young children but is NOT a reliable feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279).
There is only a small window for culture/PCR diagnosis because much of the period of organism recovery is during the catarrhal phase when pertussis is not yet suspected (p.1279).
Cross-reactivity of antigens such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin among Bordetella species makes diagnosis based on seroconversion of a single antibody type unreliable (p.1279).

Suspect pertussis in any patient with a cough not improving within 14 days, a paroxysmal cough of any duration, cough followed by vomiting (adolescents/adults), or respiratory symptoms after contact with a laboratory-confirmed case (p.1280).
Waning vaccine-derived immunity (faster with acellular vaccines) underlies resurgent outbreaks even in fully immunized older children, adolescents, and adults (p.1278).

management: Macrolide antibiotics such as azithromycin, clarithromycin or erythromycin started early to reduce infectivity and, in the catarrhal phase, modify the illness
Co-trimoxazole as the alternative agent where macrolides are contraindicated or not tolerated
Supportive care with oxygen, careful hydration and small frequent feeds, monitoring young infants for apnoea and cyanosis
Admit young infants and manage severe cases in intensive care, considering exchange transfusion or leucodepletion for marked hyperleucocytosis with pulmonary hypertension
Give macrolide post-exposure prophylaxis to close contacts and apply droplet precautions and isolation
Notify public health authorities, as pertussis is a reportable disease
Prevent through acellular pertussis vaccination, including maternal antenatal immunisation and childhood boosters
